Mörser.et: From Middle High German mörser, mörsære, from Old High German morsāri, from Proto-West Germanic *morsārī, alternative form of *mortārī (“mortar”). Doublet of Mörtel.

Morgenstern.et: From Middle High German morgenstern, from Old High German morganstern. Equivalent to Morgen + Stern.

Morgen.et:
From Middle High German morgen, from Old High German morgan, from Proto-West Germanic *morgan, from Proto-Germanic *murganaz, from Proto-Indo-European *merkʷ- (“to blink, twinkle”).
Compare Low German Morgen, Dutch morgen, West Frisian moarn, English morn, mor…

Our future is more important than our present.

morgen.et: From Middle High German morgene, from Old High German morgane, from Proto-West Germanic *morgin, *murgin. Cognate with English morrow, morn.

Mora.et: Borrowed from Italian morra, whose etymology is unknown.

Murder is, as known to every educated prosecutor, an act that is committed in utmost ecstasy and with the coldest brutality.
Mord.et: From Middle High German mort, from Old High German mord, from Proto-West Germanic *morþ, from Proto-Germanic *murþą. Cognate with Dutch moord, English murth, Swedish mord, Finnish murha. Also related with English murder, French meurtre.

mörderisch.et: Mörder + -isch, since the 15th century. Compare also Middle High German mordisch, mördisch.

s: Hart ist der Zahn der Bisamratte, / Doch härter ist die Morgenlatte.

morgens.et: From Middle High German morgens, morgenes, adverbial genitive of morgen, whence modern German Morgen (“morning”). Equivalent to Morgen + -s.

Morgenland.et: Morgen (“East”, literally “morning”) + Land (“land”). First attested in the Luther Bible as a translation of Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (anatolḗ).

Morphem.et: Borrowed from French morphème. By surface analysis, Morph + -em.
